reply: For a clear aqueous cell culture, a NIR transmission probe is the simplest, cheapest option that can monitor glucose and lactate in real time. Raman can be added later if higher specificity is needed.

recommendations.reason: Raman provides a molecular fingerprint for glucose and lactate and is well‑suited for aqueous environments, but it is higher cost and may require a more complex probe geometry.

citations.quote: Raman spectroscopy can be used in the same reactor to provide a "molecular fingerprint" for direct detection of specific metabolites like glucose, acetate, or lactate.

concept.summary: Install a NIR transmission fiber‑optic probe in the reactor, positioned to sample the bulk medium. The probe will be connected to a NIR spectrometer covering 780–2500 nm. Calibration will be built from lab samples with known glucose and lactate concentrations, using chemometric models (e.g., PLS). The probe will provide real‑time spectra that can be processed online to give concentration estimates.

citations.quote: Near‑IR vibrational spectroscopy (NIR) is the most common online analysis method performed using fiber optic probes.
NIR spectra (780–2500 nm) contain predominantly overtones and component bands of fundamental vibrations of molecules and atomic groups.
NIR spectra (780–2500 nm) contain predominantly overtones

risks: Probe fouling by cells or proteins may reduce signal quality; requires periodic cleaning or anti‑fouling coatings.
Spectral overlap of water absorption may limit sensitivity at low concentrations; chemometric models must account for this.
Calibration drift over time if medium composition changes; periodic re‑calibration needed.

steps: 1. Obtain a NIR transmission probe and spectrometer; verify compatibility with reactor ports.
2. Run a small batch, collect spectra and reference lab measurements of glucose/lactate.
3. Build a PLS model and validate on held‑out samples.
4. Deploy probe in pilot, monitor real‑time data, compare with lab samples to confirm performance.
5. If sensitivity is insufficient, evaluate adding a Raman probe as a complementary method.
